analytic.title: An Online Incremental Scheduling and Backtracking Mechanism for Time-Sensitive Networking

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: With the growth of real-time application scenarios, the deployment of Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) in dynamic scenarios has attracted more and more attention. However, since information such as the period, size, and arrival time of a new flow is uncertain, the previous scheduling results will seriously reduce the performance of subsequent scheduling. Most online scheduling methods will easily reach the bottleneck of flow scheduling, resulting in a decrease in schedulability. This paper analyzes the combinability of Time-Triggered (TT) flows and proposes the Possibility of Collision (PoC) as a measure of the degree of collisions on a link. In addition, we design a PoC-aware incremental scheduling and backtracking (PA/ISAB) mechanism to realize per-flow online deployment. The backtracking mechanism migrates the configured flows on the link based on the PoC, thereby alleviating the scheduling bottleneck while realizing the deployment of new flows. Meanwhile, we establish a PoCaware pre-routing (PAPR) algorithm to improve schedulability. The evaluations verify that PA/ISAB can effectively reduce the execution time and reconfiguration overhead while ensuring high schedulability, thus realizing fast online deployment of the network.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time application scenarios such as autonomous driving and smart manufacturing have significantly increased demand for the deterministic delay and low jitter communications. Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) is an extension of the standard Ethernet protocol. TSN switches transmit Time-Triggered (TT) flows according to a pre-designed scheduling timetable, thus ensuring deterministic delay. However, the solution of the scheduling timetable is proven to be NP-complete. Since computation time increases exponentially with the number of flows, such problems typically take minutes to hours to solve [1]. Once new traffic demands appear on the network, the offline scheduling methods have to recalculate the scheduling of all flows, resulting in a large reconfiguration overhead. This reduces network performance and consumes more time [2].

While offline scheduling methods can achieve higher schedulability, they are not suitable for dynamic scenarios such as smart manufacturing where devices change frequently [2]. In the meantime, the necessity of system recovery makes runtime reconfiguration mechanisms for TT flows crucial [3]. When scheduling new flows, the online scheduling methods should minimize interference with configured flows, otherwise, some TT flows may exceed delay or jitter limits, causing undesirable results [4], [5]. These methods usually require several seconds to complete the reconfiguration of TT flows, and even 100 milliseconds for security-critical applications [6]. Controllers in software-defined networking (SDN) technology have network-wide topology and traffic information, enabling the system to handle dynamic situations and quickly recover from failures [7], [8].

TT flows are transmitted periodically, and time slot conflicts will significantly reduce the schedulability of different algorithms. [9] analyzes the collision problem between two flows, which can improve the performance of the algorithm when all flow information is known. This study is only suitable for offline scheduling. For dynamic scenarios with online scheduling, there is a lack of suitable mechanisms to mitigate time slot conflicts between TT flows. When the network load is high, the collision problem is still serious, and the network can easily reach the scheduling bottleneck. This paper proposes a per-flow online deployment mechanism for TSN. Unlike offline scheduling methods that know all flow information in advance, we neither know the specific periods of new flows nor their sizes and deadlines. The contributions of this paper include:

• We analyze the combinability of TT flows, derive the collision probability for scheduling a new flow, and propose the Possibility of Collision (PoC) as a measure of the degree of collisions on a link. • We establish a PoC-aware pre-routing (PAPR) algorithm.

The pre-routing algorithm filters paths through the combinability of TT flows and selects paths based on the PoC to improve schedulability. • We design a PoC-aware incremental scheduling and backtracking (PA/ISAB) mechanism to realize per-flow online deployment. The backtracking mechanism migrates the configured flows on the link based on the PoC, thereby alleviating the scheduling bottleneck while realizing the deployment of new flows.

The paper is structured as follows. Section II summarizes the related work on TSN scheduling. We introduce the system model, discuss the combinability of TT flows, and give the definition of PoC in Section III. We design the PAPR algorithm and the PA/ISAB mechanism in Section IV. Section V conducts the experimental evaluations of PA/ISAB. Section VI concludes the paper.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Satisfiability Modulo Theory (SMT) is widely used to solve TSN scheduling problems, and [10] uses the SMT methods to obtain feasible scheduling of TT flows. [11] proposes a no-wait packet scheduling mechanism to compute schedules for TSN. [12] establishes the routing and scheduling constraints of TT flows to solve, which greatly increases the solution space. [8] proposes a time-sensitive software-defined network approach to schedule TT flows in SDN. [1] uses features such as flow period and size for partition scheduling, but ignores compatibility between periods. [9] analyzes the collision problem between two flows and can improve the performance of the algorithm under the premise of knowing all the flow information.

Although many methods have been presented to address the problem of offline scheduling, there are relatively few works studying online scheduling in dynamic scenarios. [13] focuses on the reconfiguration of deterministic transmissions to minimize update costs, but global network updates have high time complexity and are not suitable for handling frequent update requirements. [14] focuses on improving scheduling performance, but there are still shortcomings in solving issues such as dynamic network requirements and reconfiguration. [2] proposes an IRAS algorithm for incremental scheduling using variable time slots and an ILP solver. [15] optimizes the offline routing schemes to achieve rapid migration of virtual machines in TSN when equipment changes, but the method is only applicable to specific scenarios. [16] proposes to use the step-by-step backtracking strategy for rescheduling, but only considers the impact between TT flow routing paths. Most online scheduling works fail to fully consider the collision problem between configured flows and new flows and lack appropriate mechanisms to mitigate conflicts between time slots. Therefore, this paper designs a PoC-aware incremental scheduling and backtracking (PA/ISAB) mechanism to realize per-flow online deployment and alleviate scheduling bottleneck.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL AND THEORETICAL ANALYSIS
A. Network and Flow Model
div.p: TSN usually consists of network nodes V and all unidirectional links L ⊆ V × V between them, so it can be defined as a directed graph G ≡ (V, L). In addition, V consists of all switches and end systems and thus can be represented as V = SW ∪ ES. Fig. 1 shows the fully centralized model defined in the IEEE 802.1Qcc [17]. The communication requirements of end systems are gathered by Centralized User Configuration (CUC) and forwarded to Centralized Network Configuration (CNC). CNC calculates the routing path and scheduling result of the traffic and sends them to the corresponding switches, thus realizing the online deployment mechanism of TSN.

The IEEE 802.1Qbv standard [18] specifies that each switch egress port supports up to eight queues of different priorities and uses a periodic gate control list (GCL) to control whether the queue is open or closed. A queue can only transmit data when in the open state, as shown in Fig. 2.

In addition, the TT flow f i ∈ F is shown as a 5tuple (s i , d i , τ i , p i , dl i ), where s i , d i ∈ V are the source and destination nodes, τ i , p i , and dl i are the length in time, period, and deadline of the flow f i , respectively. We assume that all links have the same bandwidth, so τ i can be calculated by the flow size. We use φ i to represent the time slot offset of flow f i on a certain link, and GCD to represent the greatest common divisor of the periods. The minimum time unit is assumed to be 1, so all time variables are integers. Table I shows the notations used in this paper.

div.head: B. Combinability Problem for TT Flows
div.p: TT flows are strictly periodic in scheduling, and the time slots utilized by each TT flow should not conflict to achieve deterministic delay and low jitter. div.head: IV. ALGORITHM DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION
div.p: PoC can measure the difficulty of scheduling new flows on the link, so this paper designs a PoC-aware incremental scheduling and backtracking mechanism (PA/ISAB) to implement per-flow online deployment. Specifically, the PoCaware pre-routing (PAPR) algorithm first filters paths for new flows based on the combinability of TT flows and subsequently selects the path with the minimum PoC as the routing path. We use PA/ISAB to incrementally schedule new flows. If the scheduling fails, the backtracking mechanism will reroute and reschedule the configured flows on the selected link based on the PoC to achieve the deployment of new flows. Configured flows are still deployed using the incremental scheduling method.

div.head: A. PoC-Aware Pre-Routing
div.p: Since information such as the period, size, and arrival time of a new flow is uncertain, the previous scheduling results will seriously reduce the performance of subsequent scheduling. Directly using shortest path routing often leads to congestion on some links and reaches the bottleneck of flow scheduling. PoC can measure the degree of collisions of scheduling new flows on a link, so this paper designs a PoC-aware pre-routing algorithm to achieve the trade-off between PoC and routing hop count.

PAPR is shown in Algorithm 1. Initially, we initialize the new flow f n with the 5-tuple (s n , d n , τ n , p n , dl n ) (line 1). For each path p in R, we filter the paths using (5), the link load, and the deadline of new flow f n to remove unschedulable paths from R, where load n represents the load of new flow f n , load max represents the maximum load of the link on p, and the function len(p) returns the length of p (lines 3-11). We compute P oC p for each path in R, which is defined as the sum of P oC l for all links on the path (lines [15][16][17][18][19][20]. When the number of links increases, P oC p also increases significantly, thus realizing the trade-off between PoC and hop count. Finally, we select the path with the minimum P oC p as the routing path R n for the new flow f n (line 21).

div.head: B. PoC-Aware Incremental Scheduling and Backtracking
div.p: The backtracking mechanism is used to mitigate the problem of time slot conflicts. When the incremental scheduling of a new flow f n on the routing path R n fails, we infer that some of the links in the network have reached the scheduling bottleneck. The backtracking mechanism reroutes and reschedules TT flows on links with larger PoC, thus alleviating the scheduling bottleneck on the links and increasing the schedulability of subsequent scheduling. If there is a feasible solution, the scheduling result is returned (lines 1-4). In this paper, we use a method similar to [2] to establish scheduling constraints, including frame constraint, link constraint, flow transmission constraint, and end-to-end constraint. This method modifies the no-wait packet scheduling mechanism for incremental scheduling. Incremental scheduling uses the feasible solution of configured flow F c as the prior constraints for subsequent scheduling to avoid overlap in the time domain between the new flow f n and the configured flows F c . If no feasible solution exists, we compute P oC l for each link on R n (lines 6-8). Subsequently, the links on R n are sorted according to PoC, and the configured flow F l c on the link with a larger PoC is prioritized for rerouting and rescheduling (lines 10-16). If there exists a configured flow f i ∈ F l c solving fails, we try the next link (lines [17][18][19][20]. Otherwise, all scheduling results are returned (lines 22-23). When no feasible solution is found after traversing all links, the scheduling failure of new flow f n is returned (line 26).

div.head: V. RESULT AND EVALUATION
div.p: The performance of the PA/ISAB mechanism and PAPR algorithm are evaluated in this section. We use Python 3.12 for simulation experiments. All experiments have been conducted on a workstation with a 3.8 GHz AMD Ryzen7 5700G processor and 128 GB RAM.

div.head: A. Simulation Setup
div.p: We choose the Orion Crew Exploration Vehicle (CEV) network as the experimental topology for test cases, which includes 13 switches and 31 end systems [2], [20], as shown in Fig. 3. The bandwidth is set to 1 Gbps. The macrotick is 1 µs. Two nodes are randomly selected from ES as the source and destination nodes of each TT flow. The flow size in the online deployment phase is randomly generated from 125 to 1500 bytes, in the offline deployment phase is 1500 bytes, and the period is randomly generated in {0.5ms, 1ms, 2ms, 4ms}. Each group of experiments contains 50 different test cases.

div.head: B. Performance of PA/ISAB
div.p: Incremental scheduling only needs to schedule one new flow at a time, so it can improve the scalability of the network to cope with more flows, but the schedulability will be reduced. In addition, the backtracking mechanism requires changing the scheduling information of some configured flows. If the number of flows per reconfiguration is large, the network overhead will be significantly increased. To evaluate PA/ISAB's performance in dynamic scenarios, in this section we set the network to have no offline deployment phase and only consider online deployment problems. The number of new flows is set to 500, 1000, 1500, and 2000 respectively, and the IRAS algorithm proposed in [2] and the IF-ISAB algorithm proposed in [16] are used for comparison. IRAS implements incremental scheduling by traversing the routing path set of new flows, while IF-ISAB performs the step-bystep backtracking of configured flows based on the impact factor, which is defined as the number of intersection nodes of two TT flows. Fig. 4 shows the average number of reconfigured flows per backtrack for PA/ISAB and IF/ISAB. In the scenario of 2000 flows, the number of flows that need to be reconfigured by PA/ISAB is reduced by more than 50% compared with IF/ISAB. IF/ISAB uses the impact factor to group configured flows, so the number of reconfigured flows is large. PA/ISAB only migrates the configured flows on a certain link. In a high-load scenario, no more than 1.5% of the total flows need to be reconfigured each time backtracking is performed. This means that PA/ISAB significantly reduces the reconfiguration overhead relative to IF/ISAB, and therefore reduces execution time in the case of successfully scheduling the new flows.

Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 compare the average number of scheduled flows and execution time of each flow for PA/ISAB, IRAS, and IF/ISAB. In the scenario of 2000 flows, IRAS and IF/ISAB successfully schedules 1977 and 1891 new flows with 98.85% and 94.55% scheduling success rates, while PA/ISAB achieves 99.70% scheduling success rate. Meanwhile, the execution time of PA/ISAB is reduced by 29.73% and 81.58% relative to IRAS and IF/ISAB. PA/ISAB migrates the TT flows on the bottleneck links, which improves the schedulability of subsequent scheduling, and therefore obtains a shorter execution time. When the network is heavily loaded, IRAS needs to traverse multiple routing paths to find a feasible solution each time incremental scheduling is performed. IF/ISAB does not consider the compatibility between TT flow periods, so it takes more time to solve SMT constraints and reduces schedulability.

div.head: C. Comparison of PA/ISAB and Offline Method
div.p: The offline method is not suitable for dynamic scenarios such as smart manufacturing where equipment changes frequently. This causes the algorithm to repeatedly solve the schedules for all flows, thereby significantly increasing the execution time. To evaluate PA/ISAB's performance in comparison to the offline method, we consider adding a new flow to the network that has been deployed offline.

We use the no-wait packet scheduling mechanism in [11] to generate a feasible offline deployment solution. The number of configured flows is set to 100, 150, 200, 250, and 300 respectively. PA/IASB uses an incremental method to solve feasible solutions for the new flows, while the offline method uses the no-wait packet scheduling mechanism to resolve the scheduling of all flows. Fig. 7 and Fig. 8 show the performance comparison of PA/ISAB and offline method when the network has a new traffic demand. The average scheduling success rate of the offline method decreases significantly as the load increases, while PA/ISAB can still maintain a high scheduling success rate in all scenarios. In the scenario of 300 configured flows, the offline method takes 166s to complete the scheduling of new flows, while PA/ISAB only takes 0.1s to solve the same problem. It can be seen that the higher the network load, the more obvious the advantage of PA/ISAB, this is because the offline method needs to resolve the global scheduling timetable when there is a new traffic demand, which consumes a lot of time, so PA/ISAB is more adaptable to the flow demand in dynamic scenarios than the offline method.

div.head: D. Comparison of PAPR, LBR and SPR
div.p: To verify the schedulability improvement of the PAPR algorithm, we use the same settings as in the previous section in the offline deployment phase, and the number of new flows is half of the configured flows. Load Balanced Routing (LBR) and Shortest Path Routing (SPR) are set as comparison algorithms.

As shown in Fig. 9, compared with LBR and SPR, PAPR achieves a higher average scheduling success rate under different network loads. When the network load is low, the new flows are not congested with the configured flows, so the advantage of PAPR is not significant. As the traffic load increases, the SPR scheduling success rate decreases due to higher utilization of some of the links. Although LBR considers the problem of load balancing, it may still make the PoC on some links higher, thereby reducing the scheduling success rate.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper proposes the Possibility of Collision (PoC) as a measure of the degree of collisions on a link and designs a PoC-aware incremental scheduling and backtracking (PA/ISAB) mechanism to realize per-flow online deployment. The backtracking mechanism solves the problem of scheduling failure of new flows by migrating configured flows on bottleneck links. PA/ISAB uses a PoC-aware pre-routing (PAPR) algorithm to improve schedulability. Experimental results show that compared with the baseline method, PA/ISAB can reduce the number of reconfigured flows by more than 50% when scheduling 2000 flows. Therefore, PA/ISAB reduces the execution time of each flow by 29.73% and 81.58% while ensuring high schedulability.
